questions.q: Before CI exists, what does "does this change break anything" entirely depend on?
options: Whether the change passed a code review from a senior engineer
Whether the change was written in valid YAML
Whether the developer who made the change remembered to run dbt build locally before opening a pull request
Whether Snowflake automatically rejects bad changes
questions.explain: Without CI, catching a broken model or test depends entirely on an individual developer's habit of running dbt build themselves.

questions.q: What does a developer's clean local dbt build NOT prove, according to this lesson?
options: That the model exists in the project
That their SQL syntax is valid
That the exact same build succeeds from a completely clean state, since CI always builds from scratch with nothing cached from a previous run
That dbt itself is installed correctly
questions.explain: A local build only proves success against that developer's own local state — not a guaranteed clean-state result, and not a guarantee for a reviewer who hasn't re-run it themselves.

questions.q: Why does this lesson distinguish "a test exists" from "a test cannot be skipped"?
options: The two phrases mean exactly the same thing
Tests that exist are always skipped by default in dbt
"Cannot be skipped" refers only to tests written in Python, not SQL
A test only functions as a real governance gate once it runs automatically regardless of whether a human remembers to run it — that's what CI adds
questions.explain: Chapter 4 built the tests; this lesson explains that on a shared project, a test only matters in practice if running it is structural, not a habit.

questions.q: What specifically changes once a dbt project has more than one contributor, per this lesson's comparison table?
options: Nothing changes — solo and shared projects carry identical risk
Tests become optional once a second contributor joins
dbt automatically assigns a reviewer to every pull request
No single person has the full picture of every model anymore, so a mistake made by one person may be caught (or missed) by someone else entirely
questions.explain: On a shared project, the person who introduces a mistake and the person who might catch it are no longer guaranteed to be the same person.

questions.q: What real-world outcome does this lesson use as the concrete example of CI's risk?
options: A Snowflake warehouse auto-suspending during a long query
A GitHub Actions runner running out of disk space
A developer forgetting to commit their code at all
A change failing non_negative on orders.amount merging unnoticed, until a business user sees a wrong number on a Power BI report
questions.explain: This is the lesson's named concrete failure scenario — a specific, named consequence, not a vague reference to "bugs."
